Building your first block diagram

Source: vignettes/simcompR.Rmd
simcompR.Rmd

simcompR builds block diagrams in R code and simulates them. A diagram is a set of blocks (sources, gains, sums, integrators, delays, …) whose output ports are wired to input ports of other blocks. This vignette builds the classic negative-feedback loop, explains each step and checks the result against the exact solution.

library(simcompR)

The model

We want to simulate

\frac{dx}{dt} = r - x, \qquad r = 1, \qquad x(0) = 0,

whose exact solution is x(t) = 1 - e^{-t}. As a block diagram this is a constant reference r, a sum block computing the error r - x, and an integrator whose input is the error and whose output is x. The output of the integrator is fed back into the sum.

Step 1: create a model and add blocks

A model is a container. sim_add_block() adds a block of a registered type with a unique name and its parameters, and returns a handle.

model <- sim_model("feedback_system")

reference <- sim_add_block(model, type = "constant", name = "reference", value = 1)
error <- sim_add_block(model, type = "sum", name = "error", signs = c("+", "-"))
plant <- sim_add_block(model, type = "integrator", name = "plant", initial = 0)

The sum block has one input port per sign, so signs = c("+", "-") (or the string "+-") gives two inputs and computes in1 - in2.

Models are modified in place: there is no need to reassign model.

Step 2: connect ports

sim_connect() wires an output port of one block to an input port of another. Ports are numbered from 1; the default is port 1.

sim_connect(model, from = reference, to = error, input = 1)
sim_connect(model, from = plant, to = error, input = 2)
sim_connect(model, from = error, to = plant)
model
#> <sim_model 'feedback_system'> 3 block(s), 3 connection(s), 0 event(s)
#>   reference [constant]
#>   error [sum]
#>   plant [integrator]
#> Connections:
#>   reference:1 -> error:1
#>   plant:1 -> error:2
#>   error:1 -> plant:1

Connections are checked immediately where possible: connecting to a port that does not exist, or connecting two sources to the same input, is an error.

sim_connect(model, from = reference, to = error, input = 3)
#> Error:
#> ! Block 'error' has 2 input port(s); port 3 does not exist.
sim_connect(model, from = reference, to = plant)
#> Error:
#> ! Input 1 of block 'plant' is already connected to 'error' output 1. Disconnect it first with sim_disconnect().

sim_blocks() and sim_connections() list what a model holds as data frames, and the editing functions undo any step: sim_disconnect() removes the connection into an input port, sim_remove_block() removes a block with its connections, sim_set_block_params() changes parameters and sim_copy() makes an independent copy to experiment on.

sim_blocks(model)
#>        name       type   category
#> 1 reference   constant     source
#> 2     error        sum       math
#> 3     plant integrator continuous
sim_connections(model)
#>        from from_port    to to_port
#> 1 reference         1 error       1
#> 2     plant         1 error       2
#> 3     error         1 plant       1
draft <- sim_copy(model, "draft")
sim_disconnect(draft, "plant")
nrow(sim_connections(draft))
#> [1] 2
nrow(sim_connections(model))  # the original is unchanged
#> [1] 3

Step 3: compile

Compilation validates the whole diagram and produces an immutable execution plan.

plan <- sim_compile(model)
plan
#> <sim_plan 'feedback_system'> 3 block(s), 1 continuous state(s), 0 discrete state(s), 3 signal element(s)
#> Execution order: plant > reference > error

Notice the execution order: plant comes before error, even though it was added later. An integrator’s output depends only on its state, not on its input at the same instant (it has no direct feedthrough), so it can be evaluated first. The sum does have direct feedthrough, so it must wait for both of its inputs. The feedback loop is therefore valid: it passes through a stateful block. See vignette("compilation") for the details.

Step 4: run 

result <- sim_run(plan, tspan = c(0, 10), times = seq(0, 10, by = 0.01))
result
#> <sim_result 'feedback_system'> status: success
#>   1001 recorded time(s) in [0, 10]
#>   3 signal element(s), 1 continuous and 0 discrete state(s), 0 event(s)

times are the output times. They are independent of the internal steps the adaptive solver takes.

Step 5: inspect and check 

x <- sim_signal(result, "plant")
t <- sim_times(result)
max(abs(x - (1 - exp(-t))))
#> [1] 1.046722e-08

The error is far below the default solver tolerance (rtol = 1e-6, atol = 1e-8). Tighter tolerances give a smaller error:

tight <- sim_run(plan, tspan = c(0, 10), times = t, rtol = 1e-10, atol = 1e-12)
max(abs(sim_signal(tight, "plant") - (1 - exp(-t))))
#> [1] 8.902844e-13

Every block output is recorded, so the error signal is also available:

head(sim_signal(result, c("plant", "error")))
#>            plant     error
#> [1,] 0.000000000 1.0000000
#> [2,] 0.009950177 0.9900498
#> [3,] 0.019801323 0.9801987
#> [4,] 0.029554462 0.9704455
#> [5,] 0.039210556 0.9607894
#> [6,] 0.048770570 0.9512294
plot(result, c("plant", "error"))

summary() reports the solver statistics and final states, and as.data.frame() gives one row per output time, with every signal and state as a column, ready for other tools:

summary(result)
#> Simulation status: success
#> Time range: [0, 10], 1001 row(s)
#> Solver: lsoda, rtol = 1e-06, atol = 1e-08
#> Segments: 1, steps: 1004, RHS evaluations: 1467, roots located: 0
#> Final continuous states:
#>     plant 
#> 0.9999546
head(as.data.frame(result), 3)
#>   time   kind     error       plant reference state:plant
#> 1 0.00 sample 1.0000000 0.000000000         1 0.000000000
#> 2 0.01 sample 0.9900498 0.009950177         1 0.009950177
#> 3 0.02 sample 0.9801987 0.019801323         1 0.019801323
